articles.title: Trump admin tried to get free work from major law firm for arch and Kennedy Center legal battles
articles.summary: The Trump administration unsuccessfully tried to get a major law firm to do pro bono work supporting projects President Donald Trump has championed, such as...
articles.body:
The Trump administration unsuccessfully tried to get a major law firm to do pro bono work supporting projects President Donald Trump has championed, like his triumphal arch and renaming the Kennedy Center, according to a letter obtained by CNN that the firm sent to three Democratic lawmakers on November 5.

US law firm Kirkland & Ellis said it helped the Trump administration and several federal agencies with pro bono work after cutting a deal with the Trump administration to avoid a White House-prompted freeze out. But the major US law firm declined some matters without facing repercussions.

The firm did nearly $12 million of free legal work following the deal to provide $125 million in free legal services to causes that Trump supported.

"(T)his pro bono commitment was for an indeterminate period and could last beyond President Trump's term," the firm told the Democratic lawmakers in the letter this month.

Democrats have been pushing for documents to uncover information about the White House's effort last year to enlist several law firms to contribute pro bono work.

The president had issued executive orders targeting law firms — which were blocked by courts as unconstitutional — that reshaped the legal industry in Washington. The free legal work that came from the deals, which the administration cut separately with several firms that wanted to avoid being subject to executive orders, has been largely opaque.

The Democratic lawmakers are still seeking details on the other law firm deals. The pro bono work that law firms did for the Trump administration is likely to continue to be a major focus of congressional investigations in the new Congress.

Kirkland & Ellis told Democratic lawmakers in the letter that it turned down requests to work on the renaming of the Kennedy Center as well as a request to represent a veterans' group that supported the arch.

It also turned down requests to work on projects related to the Census, challenges to the US Postal Service's transmitting of ballots and representing scientists in litigation related to the Trump administration's climate policy.

The seven-page letter from Kirkland & Ellis to Connecticut Sen. Richard Blumenthal, California Sen. Adam Schiff and Maryland Rep. Jamie Raskin gives an unusual amount of detail about how the firm's deal was cut with the White House, why the firm feared the Trump administration's executive orders and the work Kirkland ultimately did for pro bono causes.

"Between February and April 2025, the Administration devoted significant attention to large corporate law firms—including both Kirkland and its competitors—and aggressively threatened actions that would have been extremely disruptive to the firms, their clients, and their employees," Kirkland's attorney Beth Wilkinson wrote, using language that signaled the firm was now willing to criticize the administration. "Kirkland took the Administration's threat seriously and focused on how it could resolve the inquiry to best protect its clients and its people."

Wilkinson described to the lawmakers how law firms worried that their clients with matters before federal government agencies may avoid hiring firms the administration was punishing, because it could create issues for the clients themselves. She also noted that Kirkland and other law firms were being probed by the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission because of Trump's crackdown on diversity initiatives.

The firm did not turn over the records Democrats sought until after the election.

"We have recently received substantial and profoundly troubling information that this corrupt bargain went much further than originally understood," three Democratic lawmakers wrote in letters to nine other major law firms that cut deals with the administration to promise pro bono work. The Senate and House Democrats are still seeking documents from those firms.

Kirkland's pro bono legal work was provided to the Departments of Commerce and Defense, the US Postal Service, the US International Development Finance Corporation and an "investment entity negotiated between the Trump administration and Japan," according to the lawmakers.

This amounted to more than 2,200 hours of free legal work for Commerce, and about 1,000 hours of work for the three other agencies, Kirkland told the Democratic lawmakers.

While the newly disclosed legal work is a tiny chunk of the firm's total pro bono efforts, the tallies are notable because of how they begin to fulfill the pledge the White House coerced from the firm.

Kirkland also has tallied contributing nearly 15,500 hours of legal work, worth more than $18 million, to the causes of veterans, combating antisemitism, other public servants and a "fair justice system," which were identified in the deal with Trump as causes the firm should support.

The firm noted it had previously represented government entities for free during past administrations, without any deals. That included helping the Secret Service sketch out practices for protecting the president and the White House and representing a Minnesota state agency following the police shooting of George Floyd.

The law firm said, however, it didn't keep records of every time someone reached out on behalf of the administration about a possible client matter, and didn't have any other agreement documents beyond what Trump had announced in April.

"The Trump Administration also unsuccessfully tried to involve Kirkland & Ellis in work supporting the President's political vanity projects, such as the renaming of the Kennedy Center or supporting the illegal construction of his triumphal arch in Washington, D.C.—raising serious questions of whether other firms acceded to these demands," the Democratic lawmakers also said.

A spokesperson for Kirkland didn't immediately respond to a request for comment on Thursday morning.

This story has been updated with additional information.

articles.title: Defesa Civil alerta para chuvas fortes no interior de SP no feriadão | G1
articles.standfirst: A Defesa Civil colocou em alerta para chuvas as regiões de Presidente Prudente, Marília e Itapeva, nesta sexta (20). Regiões de Rio Preto e Sorocaba podem ser atingidas por temporais no sábado (21), com atenção maior para o domingo (22) em todo o interior paulista.
articles.summary: Chuvas fortes durante o feriado prologando podem atingir as regiões de Presidente Prudente, Bauru, Itapetininga, São José do Rio Preto e Sorocaba, a partir desta sexta-feira (20).
articles.body:
Mudança de tempo, com possibilidade pancadas fortes de chuva para Presidente Prudente: Defesa Civil coloca em alerta várias regiões do interior de SP — Foto: Beatriz Jarins/g1

Chuvas fortes durante o feriado prologando podem atingir as regiões de Presidente Prudente , Bauru , Itapetininga , São José do Rio Preto e Sorocaba , a partir desta sexta-feira (20), com atenção maior no domingo (22).

Conforme o alerta da Defesa Civil estadual, a previsão indica aumento das instabilidades ao longo do fim de semana, com possibilidade de chuvas intensas e acumulados elevados em todo o estado no domingo (22).

A Defesa Civil colocou em alerta para chuvas, já nesta sexta, as regiões de Presidente Prudente, Marília , Itapeva , entre outras. Na maioria das regiões do estado, a previsão é de atenção.

As pancadas de chuva podem apresentar intensidade moderada a forte, acompanhadas de descargas elétricas e rajadas de vento, conforme a Defesa Civil.

No sábado (21), o alerta abrange as regiões de São José do Rio Preto, Bauru, Sorocaba, Itapeva e Registro.

As demais regiões paulistas permanecerão em atenção, com previsão de continuidade das instabilidades e possibilidade de pancadas de chuva acompanhadas de descargas elétricas e rajadas de vento.

Os agentes alertam que o período que exige maior atenção será domingo (22), quando há previsão de chuva para todo o estado de São Paulo.

De acordo com os modelos meteorológicos, as precipitações poderão apresentar maior intensidade e persistência, aumentando o potencial para acumulados elevados. Os maiores volumes são esperados nas regiões da faixa leste, norte, noroeste e centro paulista .

Diante desse cenário, a Defesa Civil orienta a população a adotar medidas preventivas:

Alagamentos e enxurradas: não atravesse ruas alagadas nem tente passar por trechos com correnteza, a pé ou de veículo. Mantenha distância de rios e córregos.

Raios e descargas elétricas: procure abrigo em edificações fechadas. Evite permanecer em áreas abertas, próximas a árvores isoladas ou estruturas metálicas.

Ventos fortes: recolha objetos soltos em quintais, varandas e sacadas. Durante as rajadas, mantenha distância de árvores, postes, placas e estruturas que possam cair.

Granizo: procure abrigo em locais seguros, longe de janelas, vidros e coberturas frágeis. Sempre que possível, mantenha veículos em locais cobertos.

Deslizamentos: observe sinais como rachaduras no solo ou nas paredes, inclinação de árvores e postes e movimentação de terra. Ao identificar indícios de risco, afaste-se do local e acione a Defesa Civil.

A Defesa Civil do Estado informou que monitora as condições meteorológicas e mantém atualizações dos modelos de previsão, em articulação com os órgãos municipais e instituições responsáveis pela gestão de riscos e desastres.

A população deve acompanhar os alertas e comunicados oficiais e redobrar os cuidados durante os períodos de chuva. A adoção de medidas preventivas é fundamental para evitar acidentes e proteger vidas, reforçaram os agentes.

Para receber alertas gratuitos por SMS, envie o CEP da localidade para o número 40199. Em situações de emergência, acione a Defesa Civil pelo 199 ou o Corpo de Bombeiros pelo 193 .

articles.title: Flávio Bolsonaro: Moraes vê obstrução e vota por restrições | G1
articles.standfirst: Primeira Turma do STF analisa recurso da defesa do parlamentar contra medidas cautelares impostas por Moraes, como entrega de passaportes e proibição de contato com investigados.
articles.summary: Flávio Bolsonaro é alvo de voto de Alexandre de Moraes no STF para manter restrições após o senador viajar aos EUA em meio a investigações de lavagem de dinheiro.
articles.body:
O ministro Alexandre de Moraes , do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ), afirmou que a fuga do senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ) do Brasil demonstra atuação com potencial para obstruir investigações em curso sobre suposta lavagem de dinheiro.

O magistrado votou para manter as medidas cautelares impostas ao parlamentar , como a entrega dos passaportes e a proibição de contato com outros investigados, caso do advogado e amigo de Flávio Willer Tomaz.

🔎Em outubro, o STF abriu um inquérito, sob relatoria de Moraes, para investigar suspeitas de lavagem de dinheiro e vazamento de dados envolvendo o senador Flávio Bolsonaro e o advogado Willer Tomaz.

A Primeira Turma do STF começou a julgar nesta sexta-feira (20) um recurso da defesa de Flávio contra as medidas determinadas por Moraes . Os votos podem ser inseridos no sistema eletrônico do STF até o dia 30 de novembro.

Moraes ressaltou que Flávio descumpriu a ordem judicial para entrega dos passaportes e estava proibido de deixar o país.

“O investigado evadiu-se do território nacional, violando o dever de permanência no país e a obrigação de entregar os documentos de viagem. Os elementos demonstram a efetiva atuação do investigado, com potencial para obstruir as investigações em curso, por meio da fuga do distrito”, escreveu o ministro.

Segundo o ministro, as investigações estão em andamento e as restrições devem ser mantidas porque são necessárias à efetividade do processo .

“[O recurso] não apresentou qualquer argumento apto a desconstituir os fundamentos apontados”, declarou.

Flávio Bolsonaro desembarca nos Estados Unidos após fugir do Brasil — Foto: Eva Marie Uzcategui/Reuters

A Procuradoria-Geral da República disse que as restrições são proporcionais, fundamentadas e adequadas. A PGR afirma que os fatos investigados são graves.

O Ministério Público Federal afirmou que não há dúvida de que Flávio Bolsonaro recebeu a notificação, transgrediu e fugiu, mesmo sem ordem de prisão, agindo com desprezo.

"A insubmissão às ordens provindas do STF reafirma a necessidade de manutenção das providências impostas, cujos pressupostos permanecem inalterados", declarou a PGR.

articles.title: ‘We’ve Got Time’: Trump Suggests Iran War Will Continue Into 2027
articles.summary: The President told news outlets that he was not rushing to make any major decisions about renewed fighting until January.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump suggested he is putting off any major decisions on Iran until 2027, amid reports that he's considering renewed major operations in the war that continues despite repeated promises that it'll end soon.

Speaking to Reuters on whether new major strikes are possible—the U.S. has engaged in limited strikes on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz—Trump, who was en route to Washington following his trip to China, said, "Well, I'll talk to you about it after the beginning of the year." He added: "We've got time."

Trump made similar comments in other interviews. "We'll see what happens after January 1st," the U.S. President told Fox News in an interview that aired on Thursday, just before his summit with China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin . He also told Axios in a phone call Thursday that he was "not rushing into any decision" on Iran.

The President initially promised that the war with Iran would only take weeks, but it has dragged on to nearly nine months, though major hostilities have subsided. Trump has previously said that the war would end immediately after the Nov. 3 midterm elections , but the impasse between Iran and the U.S. remained. And in the past weeks, he's alternated between publicly threatening Tehran and holding off on authorizing new strikes at the request of American allies in the Gulf .

Israel has reportedly tried to convince Trump of a new joint strike. The New York Times reported that the U.S. President is considering a new round of extensive military strikes on Iran, after Tel Aviv warned of Tehran's "success in rebuilding its missile and drone arsenals and advancing its chemical and biological weapons programs." Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli Prime Minister whose premiership is in limbo , is reportedly pushing for a four- to seven-day airstrike campaign on Iran.

Axios reported, citing unnamed sources , that the White House sought input from the Pentagon and intelligence experts on how Iran would respond to the strike scenarios prepared by the U.S. military. Axios also reported that any U.S. campaign would involve Israel and could include strikes on Iran's nuclear facilities such as Pickaxe Mountain, energy and other infrastructure, and Iranian military and civilian leaders.

The U.S. midterm elections, in which Democrats won control of Congress as the American public largely rebuked Trump and the Republican Party following their handling of the Iran war and the economic fallout it caused, could complicate decisionmaking. Before the Nov. 3 elections, Trump said that Iran was willing to strike a deal, but after the GOP's stunning losses, which Iranian leaders celebrated , the Administration's messaging pivoted to maintaining economic sanctions and the blockade on Iran.

Vice President J.D. Vance has blamed the war for the GOP's election losses, but still appeared to defend the President's foreign policy on Iran . The Vice President earlier said there was no difference between the President and members of his Administration on the war, but as Vance voiced his misgivings, Trump ordered the Vice President to shift his focus away from Iran diplomatic negotiations and toward domestic policies.

Trump has a small window to push through further military action against Iran before the newly elected Democrats take office in January. On Thursday, the GOP-led U.S. Senate rejected a measure aimed at curbing the war .

Trump addresses reported 'dirty bomb' threat

In the interview with Fox News, Trump said he thinks people should not be alarmed by reports of a planned " dirty bomb " attack on Washington, D.C. A dirty bomb combines conventional explosives like dynamite with radioactive material.

"If it does happen, we wipe them out," Trump said.

Trump acknowledged , however, that intelligence indicated Tehran is potentially interested in biological weapons. "Iran is looking at gases, looking at bio, because we've shut them out with the nuclear," he said, referring to the damage that the U.S. has claimed it dealt to Iran's nuclear facilities .

Iran's foreign ministry refuted Trump's recent statements. "The allegations keep changing, but the underlying narrative remains disturbingly familiar," spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei said in a post on X . "Once again, the world is apparently expected to suffer a bout of collective amnesia."

Baqaei then referred to how the U.S. justified its invasion of Iraq in 2003, alleging that the government of the late Saddam Hussein was developing weapons of mass destruction, which subsequent investigations found to be untrue.

"We find ourselves facing ominous new allegations," Baqaei said, "and a narrative that appears to be following the same fraudulent script."

articles.title: Trump can finally deliver the immigration bargain Reagan was promised
articles.summary: Attorney Mehek Cooke argues that Trump can fix Reagan's failed 1986 amnesty bargain by mandating E-Verify and codifying border security before any legal relief expands.
articles.body: Washington broke immigration and now offers America two politically convenient but false extremes: deport everyone or grant blanket amnesty. This choice prevents us from solving a problem intentionally created by decades of government failure, weak enforcement and an open invitation to abuse our laws. President Ronald Reagan’s 1986 immigration bargain granted legal status to millions of illegal immigrants, while Washington’s enforcement commitment proved temporary and inadequate. President Donald Trump can reverse that historic imbalance by making enforcement permanent and offering compassion through the rule of law. Trump has opened negotiations with Democrats while keeping blanket amnesty off the table. His approach prioritizes the removal of criminals, including murderers, rapists and drug dealers, while evaluating long-term residents with clean records and American families individually under the law. Democrats are responding to Trump’s invitation with a nonstarter: The Protect Our Neighbors Act would allow final removal orders to magically expire after 10 years and create a pathway to permanent residency for certain illegal immigrants. Due process has already produced those final orders, yet Democrats would create a perverse incentive for illegal immigrants to evade removal until they reach the 10-year mark and qualify for permanent residency. This is the definition of insanity: rewarding the failure to enforce the law and calling it immigration reform. WHITE HOUSE DOUBLES DOWN AFTER TRUMP ANGERS BASE BY FLOATING ILLEGAL ALIEN DEAL WITH DEMS History reveals why this is the wrong starting point. Reagan’s 1986 immigration law granted legal status to nearly 2.7 million people while creating employer sanctions and border funding. However, employers were considered compliant if the I-9 documents appeared genuine. The GAO found that 39% of unauthorized workers identified in five major cities used or were suspected of using fraudulent documents, and investigators often could not establish that the employer had the knowledge required for sanctions. By the 1990s, a Congressional Research Service analysis found that the unauthorized population exceeded its pre-IRCA level. Border enforcement followed the same pattern because legalization was not conditioned on control. Despite increased funding, the GAO found unfilled positions, reduced agent time on border control and failing equipment that left high-traffic areas vulnerable to illegal entry and drug smuggling and unpatrolled. The blunt truth is that compassion without enforceable security became an open invitation to repeat the crisis. President Trump holds a unique position of strength as he confronts immigration reform because he first enforced the law. In fiscal year 2026, southwest border apprehensions fell approximately 95% below the Biden-era annual average, and Border Patrol completed its first fiscal year with zero releases into the United States. Trump proved that existing law could secure the border when a president has the will to enforce it. For permanent security, Congress must codify his border policies, mandate nationwide E-Verify, impose serious penalties on employers who knowingly hire and exploit illegal labor and limit future presidents’ ability to unilaterally dismantle these protections. To prevent another failure, any future immigration agreement must include benchmarks: publicly reported removals, zero Border Patrol releases and a fully operational nationwide employment-verification system maintained for at least one year before legal relief expands. Enforcement must serve as a condition for future relief. TRUMP'S IMMIGRATION OLIVE BRANCH THREATENS TO OPEN PANDORA'S BOX AS EXPERTS WARN OF FAR-REACHING FALLOUT Rejecting blanket amnesty does not require treating every illegal immigrant alike. A cartel member and a father who entered illegally 15 years ago, paid taxes, raised American children and has no criminal record present fundamentally different cases. To be clear, neither entered lawfully, and good behavior alone cannot erase that violation, but it should matter when a judge reviews the case. Existing law permits certain illegal immigrants in removal proceedings to seek cancellation of removal after 10 years of continuous presence, good moral character, no disqualifying criminal convictions and proof that removal would cause exceptional and extremely unusual hardship to a U.S. citizen or lawful-permanent-resident spouse, parent or child. An immigration judge retains discretion, and Congress caps most grants at 4,000 annually, proving that individualized relief is not blanket amnesty. FORMER BORDER PATROL CHIEF RECALLS BIDEN MIGRANT SURGE CHAOS AS TRUMP CRACKDOWN DELIVERS HISTORIC TURNAROUND Congress should fund additional immigration judges to reduce the case backlog and deliver timely decisions. It should also create a streamlined federal review process, so each judge receives a verified case file containing the evidence necessary to evaluate every legal requirement. The solution is not weaker standards, but faster decisions and consistent enforcement. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Washington failed Reagan by trading permanent legal status for temporary enforcement promises. President Trump can now apply Reagan’s own standard: Trust, but verify. Congress must permanently codify border security to ensure no future president can simply erase it with the stroke of a pen. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP President Trump can finally deliver the bargain Reagan deserved: a secure border, case-by-case compassion under the law and permanent protection for the American people. articles.title: Republican senator opens door on possibility of a presidential bid, in shift from past position
articles.summary: Republican Sen. Josh Hawley of Missouri, who previously said he did not intend to pursue a presidential bid, is now opening the door to the possibility.
articles.body: Following the GOP’s widespread midterm losses, Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo. — who in September indicated to the Washington Examiner that he had "no intention" of running for president in 2028 — is now leaving the door open to a White House bid. "After this most recent election, I think everybody that cares about the future of the party, the future of the country, has a lot of thinking to do," the senator said to The Associated Press when asked about his presidential aspirations. "So I’ll just say I have a lot of thinking to do." Democrats delivered a midterm election drubbing and will control the House and Senate majorities next year. JOSH HAWLEY SHOOTS DOWN PROSPECT OF 2028 WHITE HOUSE BID, SAYS HE HAS 'NO INTENTION' OF RUNNING: REPORT "I was alarmed by the results of the election, and I’m concerned about the direction of both my party and the country," Hawley told NBC News when asked whether he is thinking about running for president. "And I want to do my part there. I’m trying to think through what my part is. But I certainly want to do my part for the future." "Listen, I don’t want to give you a misconception that, for sure, I have plans or intentions," he noted, according to the outlet. "What I said to you is the honest to goodness truth, which is just that I’ve got four years here to serve in the Senate, and I’m just trying to think about where I am and what’s in front of me, what can I do to help the country go forward." "I'm concerned about what comes next for the party. So I don’t know what my role is in that yet, but I’m trying to give it some serious thought, and I’m no further along than that," he said. HAWLEY ZEROES IN ON LIA THOMAS LOCKER ROOM CONTROVERSY: 'DID THEY CONSENT?' Hawley's comments mark a notable reversal, as he previously shot down the idea of pursuing the presidency in 2028, telling the Washington Examiner in September, "No, I have no intention of doing so, period." Hawley, who has served in the Senate since early 2019, won reelection in 2024, meaning his current term will not end until early 2031. articles.title: Biden memoir draws fire for ‘denial’ as critics flag Gaza, racial-equity omissions
articles.summary: Joe Biden's memoir "Promise Me, America" draws sharp reviews; critics say he stays "stubbornly in denial" about his age, Gaza, and his 2024 reelection bid.
articles.body: Former President Joe Biden’s new memoir has drawn sharp criticism and opened a debate about how Biden’s choices — and his account of them — will shape his legacy. Released Nov. 17, "Promise Me, America" defends Biden’s presidency and his decision to seek re-election in 2024. The memoir drew a sharp verdict from The New Yorker writer Amy Davidson Sorkin, who said Biden remains "stubbornly in denial," while other critics scrutinized the book's account of Gaza and what it left out about racial equity. Sorkin’s criticism centers on Biden’s response to questions about his age and his continued insistence that he could have won. "The true test of a book like this is whether its author will own his losses, too. Biden, for his part, does not," added New York Times nonfiction critic Jennifer Szalai. "He is so preoccupied with burnishing his legacy that he gets awkward and defensive when addressing the two issues many readers will be most curious about: his handling of the war in Gaza, and his decision to run for a second term." "The news of the memoir, in short, is that there is no real news: Biden is as stubbornly in denial as ever, " Sorkin wrote. BIDEN ADDRESSES INFAMOUS 'WE BEAT MEDICARE' DEBATE MOMENT IN NEW MEMOIR The dispute around Biden's recollection of his tenure centers on two consequential decisions — his choice to seek another term and his administration’s policy toward Israel during the Gaza war. In its review of the memoir, the Associated Press reported that Biden says he believed he was the best person to defeat President Donald Trump and that the Democratic primaries gave him no warning he was in trouble. Meanwhile, Sorkin and Szalai argued in their reviews that Biden gives too little weight to concerns about his age and fitness when recounting that period, despite acknowledging that his debate performance was poor. "Biden’s voice gets passive; he portrays himself as the helpless victim of events," Szalai wrote. "He gets similarly defensive when recounting the war in Gaza," she added. BIDEN ACCUSES PELOSI OF WORKING 'FURIOUSLY' BEHIND SCENES TO DERAIL HIS 2024 CAMPAIGN Self-described socialist website Jacobin and other reviewers, including Sorkin and Szalai, criticized Biden's accounting of his relationship with Israel and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, arguing he described it in the book as if it were much more adversarial than in actuality. Szalai wrote that Biden gets "awkward and defensive" when addressing both Gaza and his decision to seek another term, and faulted him for how he described Israeli victims and suffering versus Palestinian victims and suffering. She specifically noted that Biden used names to identify Israeli victims but "no names" for Palestinian victims, while calling his language about Palestinian suffering "passive." "The only consistent position is inconsistency," Israeli journalist and political commentator Amit Segal said of Biden’s account of Israel policy, calling it "devoid of doctrine or strategy. " CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Separately, Semafor politics reporter David Weigel noted that Biden recounts signing 17 executive orders on his first day but does not mention his order establishing a government-wide approach to racial equity that mandated every executive agency to develop a DEI action plan. Weigel wrote that the word "equity" does not appear in the memoir once. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "Biden argues instead that 'every one of my legislative accomplishments had justice baked in,' including 'equal access to vaccines,'" Weigel wrote. "Gender gets the same treatment," he continued. "Biden, who had called anti-transgender discrimination 'the civil rights issue of our time,' never uses the word 'transgender' in his memoir. He doesn’t mention his Day 1 executive order that banned discrimination on the basis of gender identity."

articles.title: Trump defends calling Putin a friend but says he ‘can’t speak’ to whether he's a friend to the US
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump doubled down Friday on his description of Vladimir Putin as a friend but said he “can’t speak” to whether the Russia...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump doubled down Friday on his description of Vladimir Putin as a friend but said he "can't speak" to whether the Russian president is a friend to the U.S.

Trump also insisted during a White House news conference that Putin wants peace with Ukraine , despite Russia's continued aggression after invading more than four years ago. Asked about the most recent attacks — hours after Putin met with Trump in China — Trump suggested that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Putin share equal responsibility for the ongoing conflict.

"He'd love to end the war," the U.S. president said of his Russian counterpart. But "you have two guys that don't know how to end it. We're trying to help them. You have two people that hate each other, Zelenskyy and Putin. They don't know how to end it. They want to end it. They're both stuck in it."

During a wide-ranging news conference, Trump praised both Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping after returning from China, where he participated in bilateral and trilateral meetings with his fellow heads of state.

Trump raised eyebrows on the trip with his warm greeting of Putin and repeated references to him as his "friend." He made no effort in the White House briefing room to walk back the comments. And he noticeably sidestepped a specific question about whether he views Putin as a friend to the United States.

"I can't speak to America," Trump said, without expounding.

He shifted immediately to his "very good" personal relationship with Putin and repeated longstanding grievances over the extended federal probe that concluded that Russian agents sought to influence U.S. voters in the 2016 presidential election on Trump's behalf.

"I consider him to be somebody that I have a very good relationship (with)," Trump said. "It's actually very good."

"I've been dealing with Putin" since "the fake Russia, Russia, Russia hoax," as Trump calls the Department of Justice investigation into the 2016 election. "It was a hoax made up by the Democrats" and "probably helped me win," Trump said.

Trump praises relationship with Putin after major Russian attack on Ukraine

Trump spoke warmly of Putin just hours after Russia carried out a nighttime bombardment of Ukraine, killing at least eight civilians and wounding more than two dozen, Zelenskyy said. Russia fired more than 400 drones and over 110 missiles, 27 of them ballistic and some carrying cluster warheads that scatter dozens of smaller bomblets across a wide area, the Ukrainian president said.

Putin had vowed to retaliate for Ukrainian strikes this week that severely damaged the Kerch bridge linking occupied Crimea with the Russian mainland, which is vital to Moscow's war effort. The Russian attack fit the pattern of heavy responses to eye-catching Ukrainian attacks and added to uncertainty about the prospects for the talks brokered by Washington.

Meanwhile, two Russian missiles and a suspected drone also came down in Poland on Friday in what its prime minister said was likely a provocation timed to coincide with European military exercises in his country for a possible postwar mission in Ukraine. There was no immediate comment from Moscow on the incursion or the drills.

Despite Moscow's latest aggression, Trump said Putin has expressed a desire to see the war between Russia and Ukraine end "by diplomatic means." Trump said "there's a real good chance" that a peace deal can be brokered.

Russia rejects Kushner's claims of progress

U.S. envoy Jared Kushner said on Thursday that he believes Russia is "comfortable" with NATO-like security guarantees for postwar Ukraine. Ukraine has long sought entry into NATO, particularly for its common defense guarantee under the alliance's Article 5, which holds that an attack on one member is considered an attack on all.

"I think we've gotten the Russians comfortable with that concept where any security guarantee for Ukraine would be based on Article 5," Kushner said. "And I think that that comes with at least what the Russians are saying, which is their intention is when this war is over to not have another war in the future."

But Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov said Friday that even a "quasi-membership" of NATO for Ukraine would be unacceptable, Russia's Interfax news agency reported . Ryabkov said: "We discuss security guarantees primarily in terms of ensuring the security of our own country, and that's what we're talking about."

When a reporter noted Russia's pushback to Kushner's statements, Trump brushed it off, saying that Moscow was unlikely to publicly confirm details from ongoing negotiations.

"It is also a public relations war. And we'll say things and they'll say things," Trump said.

Trump said he didn't want to talk about security guarantees for Ukraine "because we got to get a deal first." He added that the U.S. will be involved when there is a deal.

Rubio rejects criticism that Trump embraces autocratic leaders

Trump insisted his relationships with the other world leaders is key to an eventual peace.

"You know, you're very lucky to have somebody that has a relationship with the heads of the most powerful countries," he said.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who stood on stage during Trump's news conference and made brief remarks, echoed the president's sentiments, pushing back against criticisms that Trump was embracing autocratic leaders as trusted allies.

"I want everybody to understand the relationships between heads of state are invaluable," said Rubio, who traveled with Trump to Asia. "It sets the tone for the entire relationship. It sets the tone for our trade negotiators. It sets the tone for our diplomats." __

articles.title: A child support fight exposed a Trump adviser’s $15 million income
articles.summary: Jason Miller was tapped to be Donald Trump’s first White House communications director, but a scandal ended that job in December 2016 before it even began. M...
articles.body:
Jason Miller was tapped to be Donald Trump's first White House communications director, but a scandal ended that job in December 2016 before it even began. Miller stayed loyal, advising Trump's next two campaigns and regularly defending him on cable news shows.

In 2023, Miller's accountant put his total income at about $879,000. Then, Trump was elected president a second time. And Miller proceeded to make more money than he had in the previous seven years combined.

For the 12 months that ended in September 2026, he put his income at about $15 million, nearly all of it revenue from his two firms, according to a sworn financial statement he filed in court. In that time, Miller was a registered foreign agent for the governments of India and Romania and was in talks to join Trump's White House as an unpaid adviser and began appearing there regularly this summer.

Miller's consulting firm continued receiving payments - about $1.3 million from July through September, bank records show.

The details - some of which have not been previously reported and were recently included in the filings of a long-running Miami court case - offer a rare look at how lucrative Trump's return to power has been for one of his most loyal aides. And they show how much money can flow to a presidential adviser without ever appearing in public disclosures.

It took a child support fight - with the campaign aide at the center of his 2016 scandal - to bring that into view.

In a statement to The Washington Post, Miller said, "I take all ethics, lobbying registration, and financial disclosure obligations seriously and have complied with all applicable requirements."

He said he was under no obligation to discuss his financial records or his court case. Miller did not respond to detailed questions about his time in the White House, his work and specific payments, including what they were for. Testimony about Miller's income during the trial this week was first shared on social media by Grant Stern, a Democratic activist and executive editor of Occupy Democrats, who has followed the case for years.

Miller's bank records filed publicly in court show large payments from the government of India, the hedge fund Bridgewater Associates, the media company formerly called Paramount Skydance and a Japanese conglomerate - along with millions of dollars from sources the records do not identify.

His gross income had already begun to climb in 2024, while he worked on Trump's campaign; his accountant put it at about $1.6 million that year. In the 12 months that ended in August 2025, it reached about $4 million. By this fall, Miller's two firms - SHW Partners and a second company, Scipio Strategic, both of which he owns outright, according to his filing - had together brought in about $15 million over a year.

Scipio, which took in $6.7 million of that, does not appear in any public lobbying or foreign-agent filings, so who paid it, and for what, is not publicly disclosed.

Most senior White House officials must publicly disclose their finances. Miller was different. His public lobbying and foreign-agent filings - which, by law, cover only payments received for disclosable activity - account for about $2.4 million of his income over the past two years.

On Nov. 3 - Election Day - Miller wrote in a sworn financial affidavit he filed in the case that he "is currently an unpaid special government employee." Where the form asks for his pay rate, the filing says "unpaid employee." Where the form asked for his employer, he wrote "the White House."

In an unsigned statement Thursday, the White House said: "Jason Miller was never an SGE [special government employee] at the WH. We have enjoyed many different thoughts and opinions throughout this administration and will continue to do so. Our campus remains open to friends old and new, from either side of the political spectrum." The White House did not respond to further questions about what Miller's role was.

When asked about the White House's statement, Miller said, "I never completed the formal onboarding process."

Had Miller become a special government employee, he would have been exempt from federal limits on outside income and employment that apply to most White House staff, according to the Office of Government Ethics. But conflict-of-interest law would have barred him from working on government matters affecting his own financial interests or those of his clients, unless he received a waiver, said Kathleen Clark, a law professor at Washington University in St. Louis who studies government ethics.

She said his lack of official status meant he could operate without committing to follow rules. "What you are describing is someone who has not sworn allegiance to this country, who doesn't even purport to act in the interest in the public and is allowed to go running roughshod around the White House," she said.

Few people have been as close to Trump's political operation and for as long as Miller. He was the chief spokesman for Trump's 2016 campaign, and after the election Trump named him White House communications director. But within days, Miller withdrew amid reports of his extramarital affair with A.J. Delgado, another campaign aide who gave birth to their son in 2017.

He spent the next decade working his way back - as a senior adviser on Trump's 2020 and 2024 campaigns, as chief executive of Gettr, the pro-Trump social media platform, and as a vocal Trump booster. Joining the campaign in 2020, he said he was "humbled by the opportunity for a second chance to serve President Trump."

This summer, Miller started showing up regularly at the White House. Delgado, meanwhile, has sought child support from him in court since 2017; the case had never gone to trial until this month. Ahead of that trial to set regular child support, she subpoenaed his financial records.

The firms' bank statements, filed as an exhibit in the case, identify many payers by name. But for some wire transfers, they show only a date and an amount. In a summary she filed with the court before the trial, Delgado identified the senders of those wires. In Florida family cases, parties must exchange financial records, and Delgado also subpoenaed Miller's bank records; not all of those records were filed with the court. Her monthly totals closely track the income Miller reported under oath.

Most of Miller's income last year came through his lobbying firm, SHW Partners, according to his filings. Its clients have included India, as the country has negotiated for better trade terms, the hedge fund Bridgewater Associates and the public relations firm Teneo, bank records show.

Some clients had business before the Trump administration.

A foreign government, a hedge fund and a media giant

In April 2025, SHW Partners signed a $150,000-per-month contract to provide "strategic counsel, tactical planning, and government relations assistance" for India, according to documents filed with the Justice Department. India paid the firm $900,000 in 2025 and $750,000 in 2026 before Miller stopped working for the country in June, the documents show.

As part of his work for India, Miller met with U.S. administration officials including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, then-White House chief of staff Susie Wiles and others. In January, Miller traveled with Bessent to Minneapolis for a speech by Bessent to the Economic Club of Minnesota. At the time, India was paying his firm $150,000 a month to lobby, and Miller listed Bessent among the officials he contacted on India's behalf.

Paramount Skydance, through a subsidiary called Viacom, paid Miller's firm SHW $420,000 in March and June, bank records show. At the time, Paramount was seeking the Trump administration's approval to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery. The Justice Department cleared the $111 billion deal on June 12, without major conditions - nine days after the last payment to SHW. When the deal closed in October, the newly formed company rebranded as Skydance.

The trading firm Susquehanna International Group, co-founded by billionaire Republican donor Jeff Yass, paid SHW about $234,000 in 10 payments from April 2024 to February 2025, bank records show. Susquehanna is one of the largest investors in ByteDance, TikTok's Chinese parent company. On his first day back in office in January 2025, Trump paused enforcement of a law that would have banned the app.

Spokespeople for Skydance and Susquehanna declined requests for comment.

Other large payments came by wire, and their senders are identified only in Delgado's summary. She attributed about $1.5 million - most of it in installments of $120,000 - to the Brooklyn Nets. The team is owned by Joseph Tsai, a co-founder of Alibaba, a Chinese tech giant that the Pentagon added in June to its blacklist of companies it says aid China's military. Alibaba has said there was no basis for its inclusion.

The Lawfare Defense Fund, a nonprofit that has raised at least $36 million to help pay legal bills for people it considers unjustly targeted by the legal system, according to the New York Times, paid Miller's firm more than $1.4 million in fees, according to Delgado's summary - including $300,000 in late September. Miller told the Times in June that "any payment that my firm may have received from the Lawfare Defense Fund would have been for communications consulting services." The group has not issued any public press releases.

Miller's other firm, Scipio, which he started in 2025, received most of its money in a handful of large payments, bank records show. After June, when Miller was in talks to join the White House, it stopped receiving deposits entirely; the payments that followed went to SHW.

In December 2025, Scipio received a $3.35 million wire transfer that Delgado identified as coming from Celebrus Investments Limited, an investment holding company registered in Mauritius, an island nation that is a hub for offshore finance.

Miller registered in May to work for Romania's presidential administration for a fee of $300,000 as part of a $3.4 million lobbying contract held by the law firm Eversheds Sutherland, aimed at swaying U.S. energy investments, economic development and U.S.-Romania military cooperation.

Bank records show that Eversheds paid Miller's firms $2.45 million, starting about five months before he registered. The records do not say what the payments were for, and it is not clear whether they were related to the Romania work.

In April this year, Scipio received a $100,000 transfer from a sender Delgado identified as Semafor, a week after the news media company hosted its World Economy 2026 summit in Washington.

In an unnamed statement, a spokesperson for Semafor confirmed the payment to Miller's firm Scipio and said it was for consulting services related to guest bookings at events. It's a practice the company does with consultants from both sides of the aisle, the spokesperson said .

The spokesperson also said that Semafor no longer has a relationship with Miller's firm - it ended shortly after the World Economy event.

Three corporate clients - Divergent Technologies, Mesabi Metallics and OKBL USA Holding - paid SHW about $700,000 in total to lobby for them in 2025 and 2026, federal lobbying filings show, and the bank records match. But OKBL also paid Scipio $500,000, in January and June. Because Scipio is not registered to lobby, that money does not appear in the filings; the records do not say what it was for.

Representatives from India and Romania, as well as Mesabi, Eversheds, the Brooklyn Nets, the Lawfare Defense Fund, Teneo, Celebrus and Divergent did not respond to requests for comment. OKBL declined to comment.

Even before this summer, Miller appeared at events and alongside Cabinet members and other advisers. In September last year, he committed to contribute $300,000 to Trump's White House ballroom project, The Washington Post previously reported, and attended a dinner at the White House a month later for nearly 130 donors to the project.

The Post reported in late June that the White House was in talks to bring Miller on to help with its messaging ahead of the midterm elections. By late July, he was photographed in the Oval Office.

The payments continued. In the first days of July, SHW received $300,000 from Eversheds and $75,000 from Teneo; later that month came $75,000 from Bridgewater. On Aug. 18, a $450,000 deposit arrived with no payer listed. Delgado wrote in her summary that Miller testified in a Nov. 9 deposition that he did not know its source. In late September came two wires, for $300,000 and $120,000, that she attributed to the Lawfare Defense Fund and the Nets.

A Bridgewater spokesperson said that Miller's firm provided "strategic advice to the firm" but "that engagement was proactively paused when the firm learned that Mr. Miller was considering a formal government role."

Miller's registration as an agent of Romania remained active until Aug. 4, and SHW reported lobbying for three corporate clients through July 31.

By the fall, Miller was appearing at key moments alongside the administration's most senior officials. Last month, Miller reportedly interrupted an interview that Katie Zacharia, the new press secretary, was giving the Wall Street Journal in her West Wing office, telling her that Vice President JD Vance wanted to speak with them. She did not return to the interview, and her time as press secretary soon ended, the Journal reported.

In late October, Miller was part of a small group that helped secure a charter jet to fly Flávio Bolsonaro - a Brazilian senator and the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro - from Argentina to Miami after he lost Brazil's presidential runoff election, the Wall Street Journal reported. Brazil's Supreme Court had barred Bolsonaro from leaving the country. Trump has said he can stay in the United States "as long as he likes."

The bank records reviewed by The Post do not show payments from the Bolsonaro family.

Beyond the Florida child support case, Delgado has also sued Miller in New York, accusing him of sexual assault. Miller has denied the allegations.

This week, Miller agreed to pay Delgado $22,000 a month in child support, reaching a settlement in the Florida case after years of fighting that has spilled into public view.

Kevin Crowe and Scott Nover contributed to this report.

articles.title: Alberto Núñez Feijóo, sobre su cara a cara con Pedro Sánchez: “Le pusimos ante el espejo de su corrupción y mala gestión y ofrecimos una España mejor”
articles.standfirst: El líder del PP se pronunció en un mitin celebrado en Tenerife
articles.summary: El líder del PP se pronunció en un mitin celebrado en Tenerife
articles.body: En poco más de una semana tendrán lugar las elecciones generales a la presidencia del Gobierno en nuestro país. El domingo, 29 de noviembre (29N) los españoles acudirán a las urnas en una jornada que acaparará todas las miradas. En este contexto, los diferentes líderes de los partidos políticos nacionales siguen con sus mítines y entrevistas a lo largo de toda la geografía española. En este contexto, en la noche de este jueves, 19 de noviembre, se dio uno de los momentos más esperados de cara a esta cita. Alberto Núñez Feijóo, líder del PP, y Pedro Sánchez, del PSOE y actual jefe del Ejecutivo, se dieron cita para el segundo debate electoral entre ambos desde el que tuvo lugar en 2023. El dirigente popular, según apuntan los expertos en materia política, salió mejor parado que el actual presidente del Gobierno. Pues bien, el propio mandatario de la formación azul se pronunció sobre este cara a cara en un mitin celebrado en Tenerife. Feijóo comenzó pronunciándose así al respecto: “Solo hice lo mismo que llevo haciendo los últimos tres años de esta legislatura. Un relato de los hechos y de lo que ha sufrido España durante este tiempo. Ofrecí la alternativa que llevo construyendo cuatro años para que nuestro país funcione”. Del mismo modo, el líder de la oposición recalcó que se debatió con las “mismas” reglas, el “mismo” tiempo y “sin “intermediarios”: "Pudimos hablar cara a cara y los españoles vieron una realidad”, añadió. “No es el relato que le interesa a Sánchez. Ayer pusimos a Sánchez ante el espejo de su corrupción, de su mala gestión y ofrecimos una España mejor”, sentenció Alberto Núñez Feijóo ante los aplausos de todos los presentes en el evento celebrado en Tenerife.

images.caption: Alberto Núñez Feijóo y Pedro Sánchez.
Pedro Sánchez y Alberto Núñez Feijóo. AP

articles.title: Trump responds after Vance blames Iran war for midterm losses, VP says his job is to support president
articles.summary: President Donald Trump says he would launch the war against Iran again, as JD Vance blames midterm losses on voter anger over the conflict and oil prices.
articles.body: President Donald Trump said Friday that he would still have launched the military operation against Iran, pushing back against reports of friction with Vice President JD Vance after Vance attributed Republican midterm election losses to the ongoing conflict. Speaking to reporters following his trip to Asia, Trump addressed questions about whether he was displeased with Vance’s post-election assessment that the conflict drove Democratic gains in the next Congress. "I didn't say I was unhappy with it," Trump said alongside Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. "I thought the statement was fine, except I would have had one other thing that if we're asked, I would have said that: ‘Would you do it again?’ Absolutely. The answer is yes, because we cannot allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon." VANCE'S SCATHING IRAN WAR POSTMORTEM PUTS POTENTIAL 2028 GOP SHOWDOWN IN FOCUS: 'EVERYONE KNOWS WHY' The remarks followed a series of posts on X by Vance a day after the midterm elections, in which Democrats won majorities in both the House and the Senate — along with the Texas governorship — blaming voter frustration over the conflict and elevated oil prices. "The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night," Vance wrote. "If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next six years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest. But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there." VANCE COURTING DISGRUNTLED TRUMP VOTERS TO FORM ‘NEW RIGHT’ ALLIANCE AFTER REPUBLICAN BLOODBATH, SOURCES SAY On Friday, Trump called Vance's assessment "accurate" and acknowledged that fuel costs rose amid the fighting, though he said the spike was milder than anticipated. "The war drove up prices, fuel prices far less than I thought," Trump said. "I thought it would go up to $300 a barrel. You know, it's almost down to $80 a barrel right now." FOX NEWS VOTER POLL: 2026 MIDTERM ELECTIONS USHER IN A BLUE WAVE AS DEMOCRATS WIN CONTROL OF CONGRESS Despite the political fallout, Trump maintained that the military action was necessary to counter Tehran’s nuclear ambitions and to protect Israel and other Middle Eastern nations. Vance affirmed that preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon justified the political cost, while emphasizing his alignment with Trump. RUBIO DEFENDS TRUMP'S IRAN WAR AS NOT 'NECESSARILY POPULAR, BUT NECESSARY' "What I've said is the goal of keeping Iran from getting a nuclear weapon is absolutely what we need to be doing," Vance said. "It's the biggest state sponsor of terrorism. If they had a nuclear weapon, they would use it as leverage or, God forbid, they would attack and kill thousands, hundreds of thousands, potentially, of innocent people." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I think the president is the one who makes the decision, and the president has said he would do it again," Vance added. "My view is that my goal, and my job, is to support the president of the United States."

articles.title: Somali community leaders bristle at broad blame even as youth gang violence surges from Minnesota to Maine
articles.summary: Ramsey County Sheriff Bob Fletcher says about 100 of 300 young alleged Somali gang members in the Twin Cities were arrested, but many cycle back into gang life.
articles.body: Somali community members in Minnesota pushed back Thursday against blaming the broader Somali American population as law enforcement officials warned of a surge in youth gang violence. Members of the Somali community and law enforcement leaders met to discuss gang-related crimes in the Twin Cities, KSTP 5 Eyewitness News reported Thursday. Ramsey County Sheriff Bob Fletcher estimates there are about a dozen Somali gangs involving roughly 300 young people in the metro area out of an estimated 1,000 to 2,000 total gang members across the region. Fletcher said many gang members who do get arrested ultimately continue participating in "the gang life." CULTURE CLASH LAID BARE AS VIOLENT SOMALI GANGS GRIP SUBURBAN COMMUNITIES: ‘THESE KIDS ARE DIFFERENT’ "Well, many of them are [arrested]. I mean, we’ve arrested probably 100 of those 300," Fletcher told KSTP 5 Eyewitness News. "Many of them cycle out. Just because you arrest them doesn’t mean they’re not going to continue to participate in the gang life." The Ramsey County Sheriff's Office did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment Friday. However, some people at the community meeting said the Somali community in the Twin Cities metro area is being singled out unfairly. Abdirizak Bihi, a Somali American social activist, said Thursday that "we cannot arrest our way" into fixing youth crime, KSTP 5 Eyewitness News reported. "I’m concerned. I’m a father," Bihi said. "We cannot arrest our way into solving this problem for any youth. "Of course, anyone who commits a crime, we have laws." MINNESOTA HOMECOMING SHOOTING SUSPECT OUT ON BOND AFTER GUNFIRE SENDS FOOTBALL FANS FLEEING; 3 OTHERS ARRESTED Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension Superintendent Drew Evans suggested that preventing gang violence can be "difficult to measure," CBS News reported Thursday. "What a meeting like this does is it brings (the) community together in a way to really understand what the drivers of violence are to begin with," Evans said. "Prevention is always going to be difficult to measure. You're not going to be able to prove the negative if something didn't occur." The tensions in the Twin Cities mirror similar struggles in other U.S. cities with large Somali American populations, where local officials and community leaders are also grappling with spikes in youth gun violence and debates over how to confront it. In Lewiston, Maine, police reported 35 gun-related incidents this year, including 22 that involved juveniles, Fox News previously reported in October. The city houses a large population of Somali refugees and refugees from other African nations. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I don’t feel safe. I fear for my life," Mohamed Muhumed, a Lewiston teenager, previously told Fox News Digital. "I saw someone get punched in the middle of the sidewalk over there. It’s crazy." Maine Immigrant and Refugee Services Executive Director Rilwan Osman and his team unveiled a Voices Against Gun Violence program in June, which included daily workshops and community discussions throughout the month as part of a broader effort to address youth gun violence in the city, WGME reported June 1. "We are asking people to pledge that they can talk about gun violence at home in their communities, at school, outside their school," Osman said, according to WGME. The Minnesota BCA announced in an Oct. 19 news release that more than 40 law enforcement agencies agreed to "use an existing investigative model to coordinate efforts and strengthen collaboration in addressing gang and group violence." The plan also "employs county-based quick reaction teams for specialized and rapid uniformed patrol and investigative response when criminal activity occurs," according to the agency. When reached for comment about its efforts to address gang-related crime in Minnesota, the BCA referred Fox News Digital to its Oct. 19 news release. SOMALIS IN MINNESOTA UNLEASH FURY ON TRUMP AFTER FEDS RAID ILHAN OMAR'S DC HOME Former state Trooper John Nagel told Fox News Digital in October that some Minnesota Democrats have their "heads in the sand" and hindered law enforcement from stopping Somali American gang-linked violence in the state before it escalated. "They're being restrained by politicians, people that are trying soft on crime, people that are trying to send somebody other than a police officer to take care of issues, and it's not working," Nagel said at the time. Police in Eden Prairie, Minnesota, previously said an Oct. 2 shooting outside Aerie Stadium at Eden Prairie High School's homecoming was connected to Somali gang activity. About 84,000 Somali individuals live in the Minneapolis-St. Paul area, PBS News reported in December 2025. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Rep. Tom Emmer, R-Minn., sent a letter to U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen July 23 flagging concerns about the "alarming rise" of Somali gang violence in the North Star State. "I’ve said it before, and I’ll say it again. If you won’t assimilate, then get the hell out of here. First it was an estimated $9 billion in fraud. Now it’s out-of-control violence," Emmer said in a statement. "These Somali gangs have shot up high school graduations and assaulted players on opposing basketball teams with tire irons. It’s absolute madness, and something must be done." In Columbus, Ohio, police announced the arrests, indictments or convictions of 21 BL-800 gang members in February 2024, WOSU 89.7 NPR News reported. Det. Eric Clouse said that the "BL" in the gang's name initially stood for "Bantu Life" or "Bantu Love" in reference to Somalia's Bantu ethnic community, according to the outlet. Fox News' Paul Steinhauser contributed to this report.

articles.title: Trump wags finger at 'really rude' reporter, tells her she belongs in the 'back row' during press exchange
articles.summary: Donald Trump wagged his finger at a reporter, calling her "really a rude person" and telling her she belonged in the "back row" at the White House.
articles.body: President Donald Trump rebuked a female reporter at the end of a White House news conference Friday, wagging his finger at her, calling her "really a rude person" and telling her she belonged in the "back row." The exchange unfolded as Trump wrapped up a lengthy news conference following his return from an Asia trip, just after inviting White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller to the podium and praising Miller's work on immigration and deregulation. Before addressing the press corps, Trump defended Miller's temperament, noting that critics often view him as overly strict on immigration. CHINA BLOCKS BLOOMBERG REPORTER FROM TRUMP-PUTIN-XI MEETING OVER QUESTION TO TRUMP "He’s really a talent, and he’s got a big heart. A lot of people think he doesn’t. They think he’s hard on immigration, harder on this. He’s got a tremendous heart. In many ways. They think he’s got too big a heart. But we’ll talk about that," Trump said before breaking off to address the journalist. "Who are you with. Who are you with?" Trump asked while waving his finger in her direction. After the reporter replied, "Who are you?" Trump sharply criticized both her demeanor and her seating placement in the room. JOE ROGAN SAYS PODCASTERS HAVE NO BUSINESS AT TRUMP PRESS CONFERENCES ALONGSIDE REAL JOURNALISTS "And you’re really a rude person," Trump said. When the reporter tried to speak again, beginning, "So if you’re talking about it," Trump cut her off and told her she should not be seated near the front of the press area. "I’m not talking to you. I’m not telling you. You shouldn’t be in the front row. You should be in the back row," Trump said. TRUMP AND DANA WHITE HONOR MARINE CORPS BAND WITH SIX-FIGURE CHECKS IN FIRST EVENT ON NEW HELIPAD Trump then pivoted back to his closing remarks, inviting attendees to an afternoon ceremony and concert on the White House helipad with UFC CEO Dana White to honor and award money to U.S. military musicians. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "They’re unbelievably talented people, and we’re going to honor them in just a little while. And thank you for your fairness. Thank you for your questions. And Steve, thank you, J. D. Thank you. And Marco, thank you very much. Thank you everybody," Trump said as he concluded the appearance alongside Miller, Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

articles.title: Trump floats an unexpected name to be his successor as powerhouses Rubio and Vance stand by
articles.summary: Donald Trump stunned the White House press briefing room by asking Stephen Miller if he wants to run for president, as JD Vance and Marco Rubio looked on.
articles.body: During a lighthearted Friday afternoon moment with the media inside the White House press briefing room, President Donald Trump floated a new name to succeed him as president, while two expected 2028 hopefuls stood by. The president asked the media if they'd like to continue with the press conference — where Trump provided updates on his trip to China where he met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. This prompted laughs from Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who flanked him on either side during the briefing. Then, he asked newly-minted Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, whom he called the "most powerful man in the world," to speak with members of the press. MAGA VOTERS REVEAL WHO THEY WANT TO SEE LEAD GOP IN 2028 Miller took the podium and launched into a more than two-minute speech listing Trump's accomplishments from the first two years of his second term in office. "I just wanted to say that what President Trump has achieved over the last two years is more than any president has achieved by far in American history. We can stand up here for four hours and go through achievement by achievement by achievement," Miller said. He then rattled some of them off, including: "Under his leadership, the next two years are going to be the greatest two years in American history," Miller said. "And I'm so proud to be his chief of staff to oversee on his behalf the staff in this building to keep delivering wins for this extraordinary American leader." Trump was clearly impressed with Miller, who stepped in to replace Susie Wiles earlier this month following sweeping midterm losses for Republicans. "We have breaking news! Breaking news!" Trump said. "He was better than these two guys," he added, turning towards Vance and Rubio, who both also spoke at the press conference. "Do you want to run for president?" Trump asked Miller as he was leaving the podium, prompting laughter from the group. STEPHEN MILLER'S INTERNAL MEMO UNLEASHES TRUMP AGENCIES AFTER 'ABSOLUTE CONTROL' UNDER WILES' REIGN No major names from either party have yet to announce their intentions to run for president in 2028. But with the midterms finished, rumors have swirled about who will toss their hats in the ring. Vance and Rubio are widely viewed as the two most viable options for Republicans. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Miller's name has not been previously floated as a contender for launching a White House bid.
